flawed_step: The claim that being T1 implies being Hausdorff. Closed singletons do not force distinct points to have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
counterexample: Take X = ℕ with the cofinite topology: the open sets are ∅ and every set whose complement is finite. (1) It is a topology: ∅ and X are open. A union of open sets, if nonempty, contains some cofinite set, so it is cofinite. A finite intersection of cofinite sets has a complement that is a finite union of finite sets, so it is cofinite. (2) It is T1: for each n, ℕ∖{n} has the finite complement {n}, so it is open, and {n} is closed. (3) It is not Hausdorff: take the points 0 and 1. Any open U containing 0 and open V containing 1 are nonempty, so both are cofinite. The complement of U∩V is (ℕ∖U)∪(ℕ∖V), which is finite. Since ℕ is infinite, U∩V is not empty. So 0 and 1 have no disjoint open neighbourhoods.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The cofinite topology on an infinite set is T1, but any two nonempty open sets meet, so it is not Hausdorff.
